claim: Participants discriminated weak and strong stimuli with an average accuracy of 69.72% (SD = 7.94%; CI95%: [66.86%, 72.58%]).
source: Participants discriminated the weak and the strong stimuli with an average accuracy of accmean = 69.72% (SD = 7.94%; CI95%: [66.86%, 72.58%]), suggesting a moderate to high task difficulty.
evidence: Directly stated behavioral performance data from the experiment

claim: Every individual participant performed better than chance level (all p < 0.05, Bonferroni-corrected).
source: As confirmed by permutation tests, every individual participant performed better than chance level, all p < 0.05 (Bonferroni-corrected).
evidence: Statistical test results from permutation tests

claim: The average discrimination sensitivity was d'mean = 1.14 (SD = 0.46; CI95%: [0.98, 1.31]).
source: The average discrimination sensitivity was d'mean = 1.14 (SD = 0.46; CI95%: [0.98, 1.31]) and the average criterion cmean = 0.01 (SD = 0.22; CI95%: [–0.066, 0.094]), according to signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: Measured behavioral data analyzed using signal detection theory

claim: The average criterion was cmean = 0.01 (SD = 0.22; CI95%: [–0.066, 0.094]).
source: The average discrimination sensitivity was d'mean = 1.14 (SD = 0.46; CI95%: [0.98, 1.31]) and the average criterion cmean = 0.01 (SD = 0.22; CI95%: [–0.066, 0.094]), according to signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: Measured behavioral data analyzed using signal detection theory

claim: Participants pressed the response button with an average reaction time of 642.42 ms (SD = 95.79 ms; CI95%: [607.89 ms, 676.96 ms]).
source: Participants pressed the respective response button with an average reaction time of RTmean = 642.42 ms (SD = 95.79 ms; CI95%: [607.89 ms, 676.96 ms]).
evidence: Directly measured behavioral timing data

claim: The N20 component reflects excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) of the first thalamo-cortical volley.
source: The N20 component, a negative deflection after around 20 ms at centro-parietal electrode sites in response to median nerve stimulation, reflects excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) of the first thalamo-cortical volley (Bruyns-Haylett et al., 2017; Peterson et al., 1995; Wikström et al., 1996) which are generated in the anterior wall of the postcentral gyrus, Brodmann area 3b (Allison et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies on SEP physiology

claim: The N20 component is generated in the anterior wall of the postcentral gyrus, Brodmann area 3b.
source: The N20 component, a negative deflection after around 20 ms at centro-parietal electrode sites in response to median nerve stimulation, reflects excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) of the first thalamo-cortical volley (Bruyns-Haylett et al., 2017; Peterson et al., 1995; Wikström et al., 1996) which are generated in the anterior wall of the postcentral gyrus, Brodmann area 3b (Allison et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by cited anatomical study

claim: A prominent CCA component was identified in all subjects showing a clear peak at around 20 ms post-stimulus.
source: Similar to Stephani et al., 2020, a prominent CCA component was identified in all subjects, which showed a clear peak at around 20 ms post-stimulus (Figure 1b) and displayed the pattern of the typical N20 tangential dipole (Figure 1c).
evidence: Reported data analysis results with reference to figures

claim: The tangential CCA component displayed the pattern of the typical N20 tangential dipole.
source: Similar to Stephani et al., 2020, a prominent CCA component was identified in all subjects, which showed a clear peak at around 20 ms post-stimulus (Figure 1b) and displayed the pattern of the typical N20 tangential dipole (Figure 1c).
evidence: Reported spatial pattern analysis with figure reference

claim: Neuronal sources of the tangential CCA component were primarily located in the anterior wall of the post-central gyrus (Brodmann area 3b) in the primary somatosensory cortex.
source: Furthermore, neuronal sources of this CCA component were primarily located in the anterior wall of the post-central gyrus (Brodmann area 3b) in the primary somatosensory cortex (Figure 1d and e).
evidence: Source reconstruction results shown in figures

claim: Pre-stimulus alpha amplitude was higher when participants rated the stimulus to be weak rather than strong.
source: Pre-stimulus alpha amplitude was higher when participants rated the stimulus to be weak rather than strong (regardless of the actual stimulus intensity).
evidence: Observed relationship in the experimental data

claim: There was a significant difference in criterion c between the lowest and highest pre-stimulus alpha amplitude quintiles (t(31) = –2.777, p = 0.009, Cohen's d = –0.491).
source: A paired-sample t-test confirmed a difference regarding criterion c, t(31) = –2.777, p = 0.009, Cohen's d = –0.491, with average criterions of clowest20% = –0.009 and chighest20% = 0.060 (CI95% of difference: [–0.119, –0.018]).
evidence: Statistical test results from paired-sample t-test

claim: No difference was found for sensitivity d' between the lowest and highest pre-stimulus alpha amplitude quintiles (t(31) = –1.425, p = 0.164, Cohen's d = –0.252).
source: No difference was found for sensitivity d', t(31) = –1.425, p = 0.164, Cohen's d = –0.252, with average sensitivities d'lowest20% = 1.058 and d'highest20% = 1.142 (CI95% of difference: [–0.204, 0.036]).
evidence: Statistical test results from paired-sample t-test

claim: Higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitude was associated with a higher threshold to rate the stimulus as 'strong', corresponding to a bias to generally report lower stimulus intensities.
source: Thus, higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitude was associated with a higher threshold to rate the stimulus as 'strong', corresponding to a bias to generally report lower stimulus intensities, whereas the discriminability between the stimulus categories appeared unaffected.
evidence: Interpretation of the statistical results on criterion c and sensitivity d'

claim: Higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitudes were associated with larger (i.e., more negative) N20 peak amplitudes.
source: Indeed, higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitudes were associated with larger (i.e., more negative) N20 peak amplitudes (Figure 2c), as statistically tested with a random-slope linear-mixed-effects model, βfixed = –0.023, t(32.17) = −2.969, p = 0.006 (CI95% of βfixed: [–0.040, –0.007]).
evidence: Statistical model results with figure reference

claim: There was a significant difference in criterion c between the most negative and least negative N20 peak amplitude quintiles (t(31) = 2.306, p = 0.028, Cohen's d = 0.408).
source: Again, a significant difference was found for criterion c, t(31) = 2.306, p = 0.028, Cohen's d = 0.408, with average criterions of cmost neg.20% = 0.054 and cleast neg.20% = −0.001 (CI95% of difference: [0.006, 0.104]), as assessed with a paired-sample t-test.
evidence: Statistical test results from paired-sample t-test

claim: No effect emerged for sensitivity d' between the most negative and least negative N20 peak amplitude quintiles (t(31) = −1.747, p = 0.091, Cohen's d = −0.309).
source: No effect emerged for sensitivity d', t(31) = −1.747, p = 0.091, Cohen's d = −0.309, with d'leastneg.20% = 1.213 and d'mostneg.20% = 1.142 (CI95% of difference: [–0.154, 0.012]).
evidence: Statistical test results from paired-sample t-test

claim: Participants were more likely to rate a stimulus as 'strong' rather than 'weak' when the magnitude of the N20 potential was smaller (i.e., less negative), after taking into account the stimulus' actual intensity.
source: Thus, criterion c was lower for smaller than for larger N20 peak amplitudes (Figure 2e). This indicates that participants were more likely to rate a stimulus as 'strong' rather than 'weak' when the magnitude of the N20 potential was smaller (i.e., less negative), after taking into account the stimulus' actual intensity, as it also becomes evident from the SEPs sorted by the behavioral response categories (Figure 2d).
evidence: Interpretation of statistical results with figure references

claim: N20 amplitudes were generally larger (i.e., more negative) for higher stimulus intensities.
source: Importantly, Figure 2d also suggests that N20 amplitudes were generally larger (i.e., more negative) for higher stimulus intensities – thus showing an effect of opposite direction on N20 amplitudes as compared to instantaneous cortical excitability.
evidence: Observation from figure showing opposing effects

claim: The structural equation model (SEM 1) indicated statistical significance of all hypothesized effect paths (all pβ ≤ 0.003).
source: The resulting two-level structural equation model (SEM 1; Figure 4) indicated statistical significance of all hypothesized effect paths, all pβ ≤ 0.003, with model fit indices of Akaike information criterion (AIC) = 278,788.5, Bayesian information criterion (BIC) = 278,972.2, and log-likelihood = −139,372.2.
evidence: Statistical model results with figure reference

claim: SEM 1 fitted the empirical data best compared to alternative models.
source: Hence, we conclude that SEM 1 fitted our empirical data best.
evidence: Model comparison results based on chi-square difference tests, AIC, and BIC

claim: Higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitudes were associated with a lower perceived intensity when controlling for stimulus intensity.
source: When controlling for stimulus intensity, both higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitudes and larger (i.e., more negative) N20 amplitudes were associated with a lower perceived intensity (equivalent to a response bias as reflected in criterion c), as well as higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitudes co-occurred with larger (i.e., more negative) N20 amplitudes.
evidence: Path coefficients from structural equation model

claim: Larger (i.e., more negative) N20 amplitudes were associated with a lower perceived intensity when controlling for stimulus intensity.
source: When controlling for stimulus intensity, both higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitudes and larger (i.e., more negative) N20 amplitudes were associated with a lower perceived intensity (equivalent to a response bias as reflected in criterion c), as well as higher pre-stimulus alpha amplitudes co-occurred with larger (i.e., more negative) N20 amplitudes.
evidence: Path coefficients from structural equation model

claim: Higher stimulus intensity was associated with larger N20 amplitudes.
source: Higher stimulus intensity was associated with larger N20 amplitudes, which constitutes an effect of opposite direction as compared to the N20-related excitability effect on perceived intensity.
evidence: Path coefficients from structural equation model

claim: Higher stimulus intensity led to larger amplitudes of CMAP and CNAP.
source: Furthermore, higher stimulus intensity also led to larger amplitudes of CMAP and CNAP, due to the physical difference in stimulation strength, as could be expected a priori.
evidence: Path coefficients from structural equation model with a priori expectation

claim: Larger CMAP amplitudes resulted in a higher perceived intensity.
source: Additionally, larger CMAP amplitudes resulted in a higher perceived intensity, while no such effect was observed for CNAP.
evidence: Path coefficients from structural equation model

claim: CNAP did not show an effect on perceived intensity.
source: Additionally, larger CMAP amplitudes resulted in a higher perceived intensity, while no such effect was observed for CNAP.
evidence: Path coefficients from structural equation model

claim: Neither CMAP nor CNAP related to N20 amplitudes when controlling for stimulus intensity.
source: Importantly, neither CMAP nor CNAP related to N20 amplitudes when controlling for stimulus intensity.
evidence: Path coefficients from structural equation model

claim: Fluctuations in cortical processing were not driven by peripheral variability.
source: Thus, fluctuations in cortical processing were not driven by peripheral variability.
evidence: Inference from the lack of relationship between peripheral measures and N20

claim: Peripheral activity in CMAP and CNAP did not show any association with pre-stimulus alpha activity.
source: Also, peripheral activity in CMAP and CNAP did not show any association with pre-stimulus alpha activity.
evidence: Path coefficients from structural equation model

claim: The effects of pre-stimulus alpha amplitude on both N20 amplitude and perceived stimulus intensity were most pronounced around the hand region of the right primary somatosensory cortex.
source: As visible from Figure 5, the effects of pre-stimulus alpha amplitude on both N20 amplitude and perceived stimulus intensity were indeed most pronounced around the hand region of the right primary somatosensory cortex, the same region which we identified as source for the tangential CCA component used in the analyses above.
evidence: Source space analysis results shown in figure

claim: ROI analysis within the hand region of the right primary somatosensory cortex confirmed an effect of pre-stimulus alpha amplitude on SDT parameter criterion c (t(31) = –2.951, p = 0.006, CI95% = [–0.173, –0.032]).
source: Yet, a region of interest (ROI) analysis within the hand region of the right primary somatosensory cortex did confirm the observations from our previous analyses: There was an effect of pre-stimulus alpha amplitude on SDT parameter criterion c, t(31) = –2.951, p = 0.006, CI95% = [–0.173, –0.032], but no effect on sensitivity d', t(31) = 0.633, p = 0.531, CI95% = [–0.083, 0.157].
evidence: Statistical test results from ROI analysis

claim: ROI analysis within the hand region of the right primary somatosensory cortex showed no effect of pre-stimulus alpha amplitude on sensitivity d' (t(31) = 0.633, p = 0.531, CI95% = [–0.083, 0.157]).
source: Yet, a region of interest (ROI) analysis within the hand region of the right primary somatosensory cortex did confirm the observations from our previous analyses: There was an effect of pre-stimulus alpha amplitude on SDT parameter criterion c, t(31) = –2.951, p = 0.006, CI95% = [–0.173, –0.032], but no effect on sensitivity d', t(31) = 0.633, p = 0.531, CI95% = [–0.083, 0.157].
evidence: Statistical test results from ROI analysis

claim: The relationships between pre-stimulus alpha activity, N20 potential of the SEP, and perceived stimulus intensity are attributable to neural activity from the same (or at least very similar) sources in the right primary somatosensory cortex.
source: Taken together, the relationships between pre-stimulus alpha activity, N20 potential of the SEP, and perceived stimulus intensity appear to be attributable to neural activity from the same (or at least very similar) sources in the right primary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: Inference from source space analyses

claim: In a sub-sample of 13 participants, the CCA decomposition provided a component that showed a clear peak at 15 ms, likely corresponding to the P15 potential of the SEP.
source: In a sub-sample of 13 participants, the CCA decomposition provided a component that showed a clear peak at 15 ms, characterized by a spatial pattern that suggested a deep, medial source (Figure 6a). Most likely, this CCA component thus corresponds to the P15 potential of the SEP, which is thought to reflect activity in the thalamus (Albe-Fessard et al., 1986).
evidence: Data analysis results with figure reference and citation

claim: The P15 potential is thought to reflect activity in the thalamus.
source: Most likely, this CCA component thus corresponds to the P15 potential of the SEP, which is thought to reflect activity in the thalamus (Albe-Fessard et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by cited study

claim: The amplitude of the P15 component did not relate to the perceived stimulus intensity (βP15 = 0.008, z = 0.394, p = 0.694).
source: The amplitude of this P15 component did not relate to the perceived stimulus intensity, as examined with a random-intercept linear-mixed-effects model with perceived intensity as dependent variable and P15 amplitude and stimulus intensity as predictors, βP15 = 0.008, z = 0.394, p = 0.694 (CI95% of βP15: [–0.031, 0.047]).
evidence: Statistical model results

claim: Stimulus intensity showed a significant effect on perceived intensity in the P15 analysis (βstim_int = 1.851, z = 46.463, p < 0.001).
source: As expected, stimulus intensity however showed a significant effect on perceived intensity, βstim_int = 1.851, z = 46.463, p < 0.001 (CI95% of βstim_int: [1.773, 1.929]).
evidence: Statistical model results

claim: The post hoc power analysis for finding an effect of P15 amplitude on perceived intensity revealed a statistical power of 71.9%.
source: The post hoc power analysis revealed a statistical power of 71.9%.
evidence: Monte Carlo simulation results

claim: The SDT analysis based on binning of the P15 amplitudes into quintiles neither suggested a relation with criterion c nor sensitivity d' (t(12) = 1.201, p = 0.253, and t(12) = –0.201, p = 0.844, respectively).
source: In addition, the SDT analysis based on binning of the P15 amplitudes into quintiles neither suggested a relation with criterion c nor sensitivity d', t(12) = 1.201, p = 0.253, and t(12) = –0.201, p = 0.844, respectively.
evidence: Statistical test results

claim: It is unlikely that the effect of N20 amplitudes on perceived stimulus intensity was driven by thalamic variability.
source: Therefore, we conclude that it is unlikely that the effect of N20 amplitudes on perceived stimulus intensity was driven by thalamic variability and that the modulation of perceived stimulus intensity emerges rather on the cortical level, reflecting instantaneous changes of cortical excitability.
evidence: Inference from the lack of P15 effects

claim: The modulation of perceived stimulus intensity emerges on the cortical level, reflecting instantaneous changes of cortical excitability.
source: Therefore, we conclude that it is unlikely that the effect of N20 amplitudes on perceived stimulus intensity was driven by thalamic variability and that the modulation of perceived stimulus intensity emerges rather on the cortical level, reflecting instantaneous changes of cortical excitability.
evidence: Inference from the lack of P15 effects

claim: P15 amplitudes did not differ between different presented stimulus intensities (βstim_int = 0.009, t(12721.82) = 0.531, p = 0.596).
source: However, P15 amplitudes did also not differ between different presented stimulus intensities, as tested with a random-intercept linear-mixed-effects model, βstim_int = 0.009, t(12721.82) = 0.531, p = 0.596 (CI95% of βstim_int: [–0.025, 0.043]), which may indicate that this EEG-based measure of thalamic activity is generally not very sensitive to differences between experimental conditions.
evidence: Statistical model results

claim: The EEG-based measure of thalamic activity (P15) may not be very sensitive to differences between experimental conditions.
source: However, P15 amplitudes did also not differ between different presented stimulus intensities, as tested with a random-intercept linear-mixed-effects model, βstim_int = 0.009, t(12721.82) = 0.531, p = 0.596 (CI95% of βstim_int: [–0.025, 0.043]), which may indicate that this EEG-based measure of thalamic activity is generally not very sensitive to differences between experimental conditions.
evidence: Inference from the lack of P15 effects on stimulus intensity

claim: Pre-stimulus alpha amplitude did not have a significant effect on P15 amplitude (βprestim = –0.007, t(12210.50) = –0.635, p = 0.526).
source: For completeness, we also tested for the effect of pre-stimulus alpha amplitude on P15 amplitude, which was also not significant, βprestim = –0.007, t(12210.50) = –0.635, p = 0.526 (CI95% of βprestim: [–0.028, 0.014]).
evidence: Statistical model results

claim: Larger N140 amplitudes are associated with higher perceived intensities.
source: For this SEP component, a larger amplitude has typically been associated with a stronger percept of the presented stimulus (e.g., Al et al., 2020; Schröder et al., 2021; Schubert et al., 2006). Indeed, a comparable effect of N140 amplitude on perceived intensity was also present in our data (Figure 6c), as statistically tested with a random-slope linear-mixed-effects model, βfixed = –0.058, z = −3.387, p < 0.001 (CI95% of βfixed: [–0.093, –0.024]).
evidence: Statistical model results with citations and figure reference

claim: The presented stimulus intensity was related to the perceived intensity (βfixed = 1.876, z = 14.015, p < 0.001).
source: Also, the presented stimulus intensity was related to the perceived intensity, βfixed = 1.876, z = 14.015, p < 0.001 (CI95% of βfixed: [1.605, 2.145]), which was expected given the participants' discrimination performance being above chance level.
evidence: Statistical model results

claim: N140 amplitudes were associated with an effect on criterion c (t(31) = –3.010, p = 0.005) but no effect on sensitivity d' (t(31) = 0.246, p = 0.807).
source: These findings were in line with a separate SDT analysis: N140 amplitudes were associated with an effect on criterion c, t(31) = –3.010, p = 0.005, but no effect on sensitivity d' emerged, t(31) = 0.246, p = 0.807.
evidence: Statistical test results from SDT analysis

claim: N140 amplitudes were modulated by the presented stimulus intensity (βfixed = 0.030, t(30.92) = 2.275, p = 0.030).
source: In addition, a second random-slope linear-mixed-effects model indicated that N140 amplitudes were in turn modulated by the presented stimulus intensity, βfixed = 0.030, t(30.92) = 2.275, p = 0.030 (CI95% of βfixed: [0.004, 0.056]), as well as by pre-stimulus alpha activity, βfixed = 0.021, t(31.70) = 2.73, p = 0.030 (CI95% of βfixed: [0.002, 0.040]).
evidence: Statistical model results

claim: N140 amplitudes were modulated by pre-stimulus alpha activity (βfixed = 0.021, t(31.70) = 2.73, p = 0.030).
source: In addition, a second random-slope linear-mixed-effects model indicated that N140 amplitudes were in turn modulated by the presented stimulus intensity, βfixed = 0.030, t(30.92) = 2.275, p = 0.030 (CI95% of βfixed: [0.004, 0.056]), as well as by pre-stimulus alpha activity, βfixed = 0.021, t(31.70) = 2.73, p = 0.030 (CI95% of βfixed: [0.002, 0.040]).
evidence: Statistical model results

claim: The results are consistent with previous studies on the relation between pre-stimulus state and somatosensory processing at later stages, while demonstrating opposing effects for the very first cortical response.
source: Taken together, our results are thus consistent with previous studies on the relation between pre-stimulus state and somatosensory processing at later stages, while demonstrating opposing effects for the very first cortical response.
evidence: Comparison of current findings with literature

claim: Both pre-stimulus alpha band activity and initial cortical evoked responses were associated with a bias in intensity discrimination.
source: Using a somatosensory discrimination paradigm, we examined the modulation of perceived stimulus intensity by instantaneous fluctuations of cortical excitability at initial cortical processing. Both pre-stimulus alpha band activity and initial cortical evoked responses were associated with a bias in intensity discrimination, suggesting that a lower cortical excitability reduces the perceived intensity of sensory stimuli.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: A lower cortical excitability reduces the perceived intensity of sensory stimuli.
source: Both pre-stimulus alpha band activity and initial cortical evoked responses were associated with a bias in intensity discrimination, suggesting that a lower cortical excitability reduces the perceived intensity of sensory stimuli.
evidence: Inference from the observed relationships between excitability measures and perception

claim: Variability in peripheral nerve activity did not account for the observed effects.
source: Furthermore, we rule out that variability in peripheral nerve activity accounted for these effects, in line with the notion of instantaneous excitability changes being intrinsic to cortical brain dynamics.
evidence: Results from structural equation model showing no relationship between peripheral measures and cortical excitability

claim: Instantaneous excitability changes are intrinsic to cortical brain dynamics.
source: Furthermore, we rule out that variability in peripheral nerve activity accounted for these effects, in line with the notion of instantaneous excitability changes being intrinsic to cortical brain dynamics.
evidence: Inference from the lack of peripheral effects on cortical measures

claim: Elevated excitability and higher presented stimulus intensity resulted in opposing amplitude effects on the initial stimulus-related response in the cortex (the N20 component of the SEP).
source: Intriguingly, elevated excitability and higher presented stimulus intensity resulted in opposing amplitude effects on the initial stimulus-related response in the cortex, the N20 component of the SEP.
evidence: Summary of key finding from structural equation model

claim: The discrepancy between excitability and stimulus intensity effects on N20 may be explained by a common framework based on the modulation of electro-chemical membrane gradients.
source: Based on the neurophysiological principles of the EEG generation, this finding may be explained by a mechanistic link between pre-stimulus alpha activity and initial cortical EPSPs through modulations of resting membrane potentials.
evidence: Proposed mechanistic explanation based on neurophysiological principles

claim: Higher alpha activity preceding a stimulus indicates a generally lower excitability level of the neural system according to the baseline sensory excitability model (BSEM).
source: According to the baseline sensory excitability model (BSEM; Samaha et al., 2020), higher alpha activity preceding a stimulus indicates a generally lower excitability level of the neural system, resulting in smaller stimulus-evoked responses, which are in turn associated with a lower detection rate of near-threshold stimuli but no changes in the discriminability of sensory stimuli (since neural noise and signal are assumed to be affected likewise).
evidence: Description of existing theoretical model with citation

claim: According to BSEM, lower excitability results in smaller stimulus-evoked responses.
source: According to the baseline sensory excitability model (BSEM; Samaha et al., 2020), higher alpha activity preceding a stimulus indicates a generally lower excitability level of the neural system, resulting in smaller stimulus-evoked responses, which are in turn associated with a lower detection rate of near-threshold stimuli but no changes in the discriminability of sensory stimuli (since neural noise and signal are assumed to be affected likewise).
evidence: Description of existing theoretical model with citation

claim: According to BSEM, smaller stimulus-evoked responses are associated with a lower detection rate of near-threshold stimuli but no changes in the discriminability of sensory stimuli.
source: According to the baseline sensory excitability model (BSEM; Samaha et al., 2020), higher alpha activity preceding a stimulus indicates a generally lower excitability level of the neural system, resulting in smaller stimulus-evoked responses, which are in turn associated with a lower detection rate of near-threshold stimuli but no changes in the discriminability of sensory stimuli (since neural noise and signal are assumed to be affected likewise).
evidence: Description of existing theoretical model with citation

claim: Excitability modulations may be reflected in changes of membrane potentials on a cellular level.
source: On a cellular level, such excitability modulations may be reflected in changes of membrane potentials (Castro-Alamancos, 2009), which may occur in an oscillatory manner (Lakatos et al., 2005) and shift the threshold for incoming sensory information to be processed further downstream in the neural system.
evidence: Supported by cited studies on cellular mechanisms

claim: Membrane potential changes may occur in an oscillatory manner.
source: On a cellular level, such excitability modulations may be reflected in changes of membrane potentials (Castro-Alamancos, 2009), which may occur in an oscillatory manner (Lakatos et al., 2005) and shift the threshold for incoming sensory information to be processed further downstream in the neural system.
evidence: Supported by cited study

claim: Oscillatory membrane potential changes shift the threshold for incoming sensory information to be processed further downstream in the neural system.
source: On a cellular level, such excitability modulations may be reflected in changes of membrane potentials (Castro-Alamancos, 2009), which may occur in an oscillatory manner (Lakatos et al., 2005) and shift the threshold for incoming sensory information to be processed further downstream in the neural system.
evidence: Inference from cited studies on oscillatory membrane potentials

claim: Higher oscillatory activity within the alpha band is associated with a lower neural firing rate in monkeys.
source: This notion has been further supported by monkey studies showing that higher oscillatory activity within the alpha band is associated with a lower neural firing rate (Bollimunta et al., 2011; Haegens et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited monkey studies

claim: Amplitude fluctuations of the N20 component have been found to relate to pre-stimulus alpha activity both at a given instance and through their long-term temporal dynamics.
source: Notably, amplitude fluctuations of the N20 component have recently been found to relate to pre-stimulus alpha activity both at a given instance and through their long-term temporal dynamics, which suggests that both measures reflect a common modulating factor, that is, cortical excitability (Stephani et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited study

claim: Pre-stimulus alpha activity and N20 amplitude fluctuations reflect a common modulating factor, that is, cortical excitability.
source: Notably, amplitude fluctuations of the N20 component have recently been found to relate to pre-stimulus alpha activity both at a given instance and through their long-term temporal dynamics, which suggests that both measures reflect a common modulating factor, that is, cortical excitability (Stephani et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference from cited study

claim: Instantaneous excitability fluctuations affect sensory brain responses already at earliest possible cortical processing with behaviorally relevant consequences.
source: Our results show that both pre-stimulus alpha activity and N20 amplitudes are associated with a bias in the perceived intensity of somatosensory stimuli. Thus, instantaneous excitability fluctuations affect sensory brain responses already at earliest possible cortical processing with behaviorally relevant consequences.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: Elevated neural excitability and stronger stimulus intensity resulted in reverse effects on short-latency SEP amplitudes.
source: Counter-intuitively, elevated neural excitability and stronger stimulus intensity resulted in reverse effects on short-latency SEP amplitudes, which in turn may offer further insights into the neural mechanisms of excitability regulation through resting membrane potentials.
evidence: Summary of key finding

claim: The opposing effects of excitability and stimulus intensity on SEP amplitudes may offer insights into the neural mechanisms of excitability regulation through resting membrane potentials.
source: Counter-intuitively, elevated neural excitability and stronger stimulus intensity resulted in reverse effects on short-latency SEP amplitudes, which in turn may offer further insights into the neural mechanisms of excitability regulation through resting membrane potentials.
evidence: Speculation about implications of findings

claim: Effects of pre-stimulus oscillatory activity on the processing of sensory stimuli are not restricted to near-threshold stimuli.
source: Furthermore, these findings demonstrate that effects of pre-stimulus oscillatory activity on the processing of sensory stimuli are not restricted to near-threshold stimuli where a detection threshold is assumed to be shifted by ongoing brain activity (Iemi et al., 2017; Samaha et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference from current findings compared to previous literature

claim: Cortical excitability can affect the representation of stimulus features in supra-threshold perception.
source: Instead, our findings suggest that cortical excitability can affect the representation of stimulus features in supra-threshold perception, too.
evidence: Inference from current findings

claim: The criterion-free discrimination paradigm of two neutral response alternatives precluded the potential confounding effect of perceptual confidence.
source: Importantly, our criterion-free discrimination paradigm of two neutral response alternatives ('strong' or 'weak') precluded the potential confounding effect of perceptual confidence, which has recently been considered as an alternative explanation for pre-stimulus alpha effects on perceptual biases (Benwell et al., 2017; Samaha et al., 2017).
evidence: Methodological design feature with citations to alternative explanations

claim: Pre-stimulus alpha oscillations affect the behavioral outcome via a modulation of the internally represented stimulus intensity.
source: Thus, the current findings unequivocally indicate – to the best of our knowledge for the first time – that pre-stimulus alpha oscillations affect the behavioral outcome via a modulation of the internally represented stimulus intensity.
evidence: Inference from current findings

claim: An increase in N_neurons should lead to an increase of SEP amplitude with stimulus intensity.
source: This should lead to an increase of SEP amplitude with stimulus intensity, as reported in previous studies (Jousmäki and Forss, 1998; Klostermann et al., 1998) and as was observed in the current dataset for cortical (Figure 2d) as well as peripheral responses (Figure 3b and d).
evidence: Inference supported by citations and current data

claim: EPSCs directly depend on the electro-chemical driving forces produced by the membrane potential.
source: Crucially, EPSCs directly depend on the electro-chemical driving forces produced by the membrane potential.
evidence: Established neurophysiological principle

claim: When moving the membrane potential toward depolarization (a state of higher excitability), the electro-chemical driving force for further depolarizing inward trans-membrane currents is decreased.
source: When moving the membrane potential toward depolarization – a state of higher excitability – the electro-chemical driving force for further depolarizing inward trans-membrane currents is decreased (Castro-Alamancos, 2009), which leads to smaller EPSCs (Deisz et al., 1991), and should in turn result in smaller amplitudes of the scalp EEG.
evidence: Supported by cited studies on membrane biophysics

claim: Decreased electro-chemical driving force leads to smaller EPSCs.
source: When moving the membrane potential toward depolarization – a state of higher excitability – the electro-chemical driving force for further depolarizing inward trans-membrane currents is decreased (Castro-Alamancos, 2009), which leads to smaller EPSCs (Deisz et al., 1991), and should in turn result in smaller amplitudes of the scalp EEG.
evidence: Supported by cited study

claim: Smaller EPSCs should result in smaller amplitudes of the scalp EEG.
source: When moving the membrane potential toward depolarization – a state of higher excitability – the electro-chemical driving force for further depolarizing inward trans-membrane currents is decreased (Castro-Alamancos, 2009), which leads to smaller EPSCs (Deisz et al., 1991), and should in turn result in smaller amplitudes of the scalp EEG.
evidence: Logical inference from the chain of physiological mechanisms

claim: Assuming an inverse relationship between the amplitude of alpha oscillations and neuronal excitability, one should expect decreased N20 amplitudes following low pre-stimulus alpha activity.
source: Assuming an inverse relationship between the amplitude of alpha oscillations and neuronal excitability (as for example indicated by a lower neural firing rate during higher alpha activity; Haegens et al., 2011), one should hence rather expect decreased N20 amplitudes following low pre-stimulus alpha activity.
evidence: Logical inference from the proposed mechanism with citation

claim: Smaller (i.e., less negative) N20 amplitudes reflect a state of higher excitability.
source: Moreover, the notion of smaller (i.e., less negative) N20 amplitudes reflecting a state of higher excitability is corroborated by the behavioral data: When controlling for stimulus intensity, we found smaller N20 amplitudes to be associated with higher perceived stimulus intensity.
evidence: Inference from the relationship between N20 and perception

claim: The attenuation of early SEPs during high excitability states is in line with previous observations from biophysically realistic modeling of oscillatory activity in the somatosensory cortex.
source: Notably, the attenuation of early SEPs during high excitability states is in fact in line with previous observations from biophysically realistic modeling of oscillatory activity in the somatosensory cortex as well as its interplay with stimulus-evoked responses (Jones et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited modeling study

claim: The intensity of the presented stimulus and the degree of instantaneous neural excitability are jointly reflected in the early SEP but with opposing signatures.
source: Taken together, our findings thus demonstrate that the intensity of the presented stimulus and the degree of instantaneous neural excitability are jointly reflected in the early SEP but with opposing signatures: While stronger stimulus intensity increases the N20 potential, decreased N20 amplitudes appear to be associated with an increase in excitability (which in turn lead to a higher perceived stimulus intensity).
evidence: Summary of key findings

claim: The amplitude of early event-related potentials may reflect the size of the input, but the neural evaluation of this input depends on internal neural states such as neural excitability.
source: Rather, our findings call for a more differentiated view. Although the amplitude of early event-related potentials may indeed reflect the size of the input (e.g., a stronger or weaker somatosensory stimulus), the neural evaluation of this input (i.e., the perceived intensity), however, further depends on internal neural states, such as neural excitability, which may even reverse the amplitude effects of the input already at the earliest cortical processing stages.
evidence: Inference from current findings

claim: Internal neural states such as neural excitability may reverse the amplitude effects of the input already at the earliest cortical processing stages.
source: Although the amplitude of early event-related potentials may indeed reflect the size of the input (e.g., a stronger or weaker somatosensory stimulus), the neural evaluation of this input (i.e., the perceived intensity), however, further depends on internal neural states, such as neural excitability, which may even reverse the amplitude effects of the input already at the earliest cortical processing stages.
evidence: Inference from current findings

claim: The present findings of opposing signatures of neural excitability and sensory input appear to be a distinct characteristic of early cortical potentials, involving the first bottom-up sensory processing.
source: Thus, the present findings of opposing signatures of neural excitability and sensory input appear to be a distinct characteristic of early cortical potentials, involving the first bottom-up sensory processing.
evidence: Inference from comparison of early and late SEP components

claim: The proposed physiological model may be directly applicable to well-isolated neural signals only (such as the N20 component of the SEP).
source: In this context, it should be further emphasized that our proposed physiological model may be directly applicable to well-isolated neural signals only (such as the N20 component of the SEP).
evidence: Limitation of the proposed model

claim: The physiological interpretation of amplitudes of later EEG potentials, such as the N140, is not as straightforward as for the N20 since several distinct SEP components may interact.
source: The physiological interpretation of amplitudes of later EEG potentials, such as the N140, however, is not as straightforward as described above, since several distinct SEP components may interact (Auksztulewicz et al., 2012), and excitatory and inhibitory contributions cannot be readily distinguished.
evidence: Limitation noted with citation

claim: With the present data, we cannot unambiguously conclude that the observed relation between pre-stimulus alpha activity and initial SEP involved the very same neuronal populations.
source: Furthermore, with the present data, we cannot unambiguously conclude that the observed relation between pre-stimulus alpha activity and initial SEP indeed involved the very same neuronal populations – which may represent a limitation of the hypothesized mechanism.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the study

claim: All approaches to localize the effects pointed to very similar cortical regions.
source: However, all approaches to localize these effects pointed to very similar cortical regions (as discussed in the following section).
evidence: Summary of source localization results

claim: The presented mechanism reflects a hypothesized model, which shall be further supported or falsified with more targeted studies.
source: Also, we would like to emphasize that the presented mechanism reflects a hypothesized model, which shall be further supported or falsified with more targeted studies, for example, directly quantifying membrane potentials and trans-membrane currents in relation to different excitability states in somatosensation.
evidence: Acknowledgment of the speculative nature of the proposed mechanism

claim: Variability in afferent peripheral activity, as measured by CNAP at the upper arm, did not influence the perceived stimulus intensity when controlling for stimulus intensity.
source: Variability in afferent peripheral activity, as measured by CNAP at the upper arm, did not influence the perceived stimulus intensity when controlling for stimulus intensity.
evidence: Results from structural equation model

claim: A robust effect on the perceived stimulus intensity was observed for efferent peripheral activity, as measured by CMAP of the M. abductor pollicis brevis.
source: However, a robust effect on the perceived stimulus intensity was observed for efferent peripheral activity, as measured by CMAP of the M. abductor pollicis brevis.
evidence: Results from structural equation model

claim: The CMAP effect on perceived intensity may be explained by differences in proprioceptive sensations associated with the thumb twitches elicited by the stimulation.
source: This may be explained by differences in proprioceptive sensations associated with the thumb twitches elicited by the stimulation, whose extent may depend on changes of the prevailing muscle tonus.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the CMAP effect

claim: The excitability effects in the early SEP are distinct from variability in peripheral nerve activity.
source: Thus, the excitability effects in the early SEP are distinct from variability in peripheral nerve activity.
evidence: Inference from the lack of relationship between peripheral measures and N20

claim: Pre-stimulus alpha band activity and the N20 component of the SEP were retrieved from the same neuronal sources.
source: Furthermore, pre-stimulus alpha band activity and the N20 component of the SEP were retrieved from the same neuronal sources, which – as indicated by source reconstruction of the tangential CCA components – were localized in the primary sensory cortex, centered around the hand region of Brodmann area 3b.
evidence: Source reconstruction results

claim: The findings support the notion of excitability fluctuations in primary sensory regions of the cortex, being reflected in both ongoing and evoked neural activity.
source: Although one should bear in mind the limited spatial resolution of EEG, this further supports the notion of excitability fluctuations in primary sensory regions of the cortex, being reflected in both ongoing and evoked neural activity.
evidence: Inference from source space analyses with acknowledgment of methodological limitation

claim: It remains an open question whether the observed excitability changes reflect local or global neural dynamics.
source: However, it remains an open question whether the observed excitability changes reflect local or global neural dynamics.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation and open question

claim: There is initial evidence that cortical excitability may be organized temporally in a scale-free manner.
source: Although there is initial evidence that cortical excitability may be organized temporally in a scale-free manner (Stephani et al., 2020), which may reflect an embedding into global critical-state dynamics (Avramiea et al., 2020; Beggs and Plenz, 2003; Palva et al., 2013), future work has to examine the spatial organization of excitability more specifically across different somatotopic projections in primary sensory areas as well as across diverse brain regions.
evidence: Cited evidence with speculation about future research

claim: It is unclear how exactly the observed fluctuations of initial cortical responses are integrated in later, downstream neural processes.
source: In addition, it is unclear at this point how exactly the observed fluctuations of initial cortical responses are integrated in later, downstream neural processes.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation and open question

claim: Changes in early sensory processing should provide the ground for later neural activity involved in the perceptual decision making, and finally shape the behavioral outcome.
source: In principle, changes in early sensory processing should provide the ground for later neural activity involved in the perceptual decision making, and finally shape the behavioral outcome (as observed in the current study).
evidence: Logical inference with reference to current findings

claim: With the current data, we cannot unambiguously tell whether the modulation of alpha oscillations may reflect a top-down regulated signal.
source: However, with our data, we cannot unambiguously tell whether the modulation of alpha oscillations – associated with excitability changes at the earliest cortical level – may in turn reflect a top-down regulated signal, which could enable the neural system to account for ongoing fluctuations of excitability and even benefit from a certain degree of variability.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation and speculation

claim: More and more evidence suggests an adaptive, functional role of neural 'noise'.
source: Although more and more evidence indeed suggest an adaptive, functional role of neural 'noise' (e.g., Findling and Wyart, 2021), further studies are needed to better understand how this concept may pertain also to such fundamental neural properties as the initial cortical excitability to external sensory stimuli.
evidence: Cited evidence with speculation about future research

claim: Fluctuations of neural excitability shaped the perceived stimulus intensity already during the very first cortical response (at ~20 ms).
source: Fluctuations of neural excitability shaped the perceived stimulus intensity already during the very first cortical response (at ~20 ms) yet demonstrating opposite neural signatures as compared to the effect of presented stimulus intensity.
evidence: Summary of main finding from abstract

claim: The findings call for reconsidering conventional interpretations of brain potential magnitudes in stimulus intensity encoding.
source: We reconcile this discrepancy via a common framework based on the modulation of electro-chemical membrane gradients linking neural states and responses, which calls for reconsidering conventional interpretations of brain potential magnitudes in stimulus intensity encoding.
evidence: Implication of findings from abstract

claim: A total of 32 participants (all male, mean age = 27.0 years, SD = 5.0) were recruited.
source: A total of 32 participants (all male, mean age = 27.0 years, SD = 5.0) were recruited from the database of the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences, Leipzig, Germany.
evidence: Participant demographics

claim: All participants were right-handed with a mean lateralization score of +93.1 (SD = 11.6).
source: As assessed using the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971), all participants were right-handed (lateralization score, M = + 93.1, SD = 11.6).
evidence: Participant characteristics with citation

claim: The intensity of the weak stimulus was set to 1.2 times the motor threshold.
source: The intensity of the weak stimulus was set to 1.2 times the motor threshold, leading to a clearly visible thumb twitch for every stimulus.
evidence: Experimental parameter

claim: The intensity of the strong stimulus was adjusted to be barely above the just-noticeable difference, corresponding to a discrimination sensitivity of about d' = 1.5.
source: The intensity of the strong stimulus was adjusted during training blocks prior to the experiment so that it was barely above the just-noticeable difference, corresponding to a discrimination sensitivity of about d' = 1.5 according to Signal Detection Theory (SDT; Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: Experimental parameter with citation

claim: The average stimulation intensities were 6.60 mA (SD = 1.62) for the weak stimulus and 7.93 mA (SD = 2.06) for the strong stimulus.
source: Thus, the stimulation intensities of the two stimuli were only barely distinguishable (despite both being clearly perceivable), with average intensities of 6.60 mA (SD = 1.62) and 7.93 mA (SD = 2.06), for the weak and strong stimulus, respectively.
evidence: Measured experimental parameters

claim: Inter-stimulus intervals ranged from 1463 to 1563 ms with an average of 1513 ms.
source: Weak and strong stimuli were presented with an equal probability in a continuous, pseudo-randomized sequence with inter-stimulus intervals (ISI) ranging from 1463 to 1563 ms (randomly drawn from a uniform distribution; ISIaverage = 1513 ms).
evidence: Experimental timing parameters

claim: In total, 1000 stimuli were applied, divided into five blocks of 200 stimuli each.
source: In total, 1000 stimuli were applied, divided into five blocks of 200 stimuli each with short breaks in between.
evidence: Experimental design details

claim: EEG data were recorded from 60 Ag/AgCl electrodes at a sampling rate of 5000 Hz.
source: EEG data were recorded from 60 Ag/AgCl electrodes at a sampling rate of 5000 Hz using an 80-channel EEG system (NeurOne Tesla, Bittium, Oulu, Finland).
evidence: Data acquisition parameters
